records.topic: The Control Room That Keeps GPS Honest
records.coreQuestion: Why does every GPS fix on Earth depend on a control station correcting clocks in orbit?
records.openingLine: GPS clocks drift 38 microseconds every day.
records.secondBeat: Without correction, your position would slide away within hours.
records.dependency: Every GPS position and timing signal depends on the control segment keeping satellite clocks and orbits corrected.
records.mechanism: Monitor stations track the satellites; the master control station computes clock and orbit corrections and uploads them through ground antennas.
records.bottleneck: The control segment is a single military-run system whose corrections every receiver silently trusts.
records.failureConsequence: If uploads stopped, broadcast clock and orbit data would age and position errors would grow day by day.
records.resilience: Backup master control, worldwide monitor stations and other satellite navigation systems limit the risk.
records.expectedConsequence: errors grow gradually rather than switching off at once
editorialTitles: The Hidden Correction Behind Every GPS Fix
Why GPS Satellites' Clocks Run Fast

facts.claim: Relativity predicts that clocks on GPS satellites, as observed from Earth, run 38 microseconds faster per day.
The full constellation of 24 satellites became operational in 1993.
Beginning in 1988, command and control moved to the 2nd Satellite Control Squadron at Schriever Space Force Base in Colorado.
A timing error of 1 nanosecond corresponds to a positional error of roughly 30 cm.
GPS monitor stations include Hawaii, Kwajalein Atoll, Ascension Island, Diego Garcia and Cape Canaveral.

narration.text: GPS clocks drift 38 microseconds every day.
Without correction, your position would slide away within hours.
One nanosecond of error means about 30 centimetres of position error.
Relativity makes satellite clocks run fast compared with ours.
So monitor stations from Hawaii to Diego Garcia watch every satellite.
A control squadron in Colorado computes and uploads the fixes.
That's why your phone depends on a control room you'll never see.

records.topic: The Atomic Clocks Flying Above Your Phone
records.coreQuestion: Why does a nanosecond of clock error in orbit become a position error on the ground?
records.openingLine: Your map depends on atomic clocks in orbit.
records.secondBeat: One nanosecond wrong puts you 30 centimetres off.
records.dependency: Satellite positioning depends on onboard atomic clocks keeping nanosecond-level time.
records.mechanism: Receivers measure how long each satellite's timestamped signal took to arrive; clock errors turn directly into distance errors at the speed of light.
records.bottleneck: Space-qualified atomic clocks are specialised instruments that cannot be repaired once launched.
records.failureConsequence: A failing satellite clock corrupts ranging from that satellite until controllers flag it unhealthy or switch clocks.
records.resilience: Each satellite carries redundant clocks, and ground control can mark a faulty satellite unusable within minutes.
records.expectedConsequence: one bad clock degrades accuracy until it is excluded
editorialTitles: Why a Nanosecond Matters to Your Map
The Atomic Clocks Orbiting Above You

facts.claim: A timing error of 1 nanosecond corresponds to a positional error of roughly 30 cm when multiplied by the speed of light.
Following the 2019 revision of the SI, every base unit except the mole relies on the definition of the second.
Clocks on GPS satellites, as observed from Earth, run 38 microseconds faster per day.
The second is expected to be redefined when optical clocks mature, around 2030 or 2034.
In 1955 Friedwardt Winterberg proposed testing general relativity with atomic clocks placed in orbit.

narration.text: Your map depends on atomic clocks in orbit.
One nanosecond wrong puts you 30 centimetres off.
Your receiver times how long each signal took to arrive.
Light covers about 30 centimetres every nanosecond.
And orbiting clocks gain 38 microseconds a day from relativity.
Once launched, those clocks can never be repaired.
That's why every navigation satellite carries atomic clocks.

records.topic: The Spinning Wheels That Point Space Telescopes
records.coreQuestion: How did two failed spinning wheels end a planet-hunting telescope's main mission?
records.openingLine: Kepler lost its aim when two wheels failed.
records.secondBeat: They were reaction wheels, which point spacecraft.
records.dependency: Precise spacecraft pointing depends on reaction wheels that turn the craft without using fuel.
records.mechanism: Spinning a wheel one way turns the spacecraft the other way, conserving angular momentum.
records.bottleneck: Wheels wear out in space, and most spacecraft cannot be serviced when they do.
records.failureConsequence: Losing wheels below the needed minimum ends precise pointing, forcing thrusters or a reduced mission.
records.resilience: Spare wheels, redundant designs and clever operations like Kepler's K2 mission recover some capability.
records.expectedConsequence: precision pointing is lost first; missions survive only in degraded modes
editorialTitles: How Two Wheels Ended Kepler's Mission
The Spinning Wheels That Aim Spacecraft

facts.claim: From July 2012 to May 11, 2013, two out of the four reaction wheels in the Kepler space telescope failed.
On August 15, 2013, engineers concluded Kepler's reaction wheels could not be recovered and transit planet-searching could not continue.
On May 16, 2014, NASA extended Kepler into a new mission named K2.
Hubble was designed with four redundant wheels and keeps pointing ability as long as three are functional.
Hayabusa's X-axis reaction wheel failed in 2004 and its Y-axis wheel failed in 2005.

narration.text: Kepler lost its aim when two wheels failed.
They were reaction wheels, which point spacecraft.
Spin a wheel one way, and the craft turns the other.
Kepler had four. Two failed between 2012 and 2013.
Without them, it couldn't hold steady enough to find planets.
Hubble needs three of its four, and astronauts have replaced wheels.
That's why a spinning wheel can decide a mission's life.

records.topic: The 40,000 Objects Someone Has to Track
records.coreQuestion: How do satellites avoid collisions with tens of thousands of tracked objects in orbit?
records.openingLine: 40,230 objects in orbit are being tracked.
records.secondBeat: Every satellite's safety depends on knowing where they are.
records.dependency: Collision avoidance for every satellite depends on space surveillance networks cataloguing debris.
records.mechanism: Radars and telescopes track objects, predict close approaches, and operators manoeuvre when the collision risk is high enough.
records.bottleneck: Only objects large enough to be tracked can be avoided; smaller fragments remain invisible hazards.
records.failureConsequence: Without tracking, operators could not see coming conjunctions, and each collision would create more debris.
records.resilience: Multiple national and commercial tracking networks, data sharing and debris-mitigation rules reduce the risk.
records.expectedConsequence: collision risk rises quietly; the damage appears as new debris clouds
editorialTitles: The 40,000 Objects Circling Earth
Why Satellites Dodge Space Junk

facts.claim: As of April 2025, ESA reported 40,230 artificial objects in orbit regularly tracked by space surveillance networks.
As of 2009, more than 13,000 close calls were tracked weekly.
Known debris with a collision chance over 1/10,000 is avoided by manoeuvring the space station.
In 2011, NASA said that 22,000 objects were being tracked.
In 1981 the number of objects in orbit was estimated at 5,000.
By the late 1990s, about 8,500 of 28,000 launched objects remained in orbit.

narration.text: 40,230 objects in orbit are being tracked.
Every satellite's safety depends on knowing where they are.
In 1981, the estimate was about 5,000.
By 2009, over 13,000 close calls were logged every week.
The space station moves when the collision risk tops one in 10,000.
But fragments too small to track can't be dodged at all.
That's why tracking networks quietly protect every satellite you use.

records.topic: Three Antenna Sites Hear Every Deep-Space Probe
records.coreQuestion: How do three antenna complexes keep contact with spacecraft across the Solar System?
records.openingLine: Why every deep-space probe depends on 3 sites.
records.secondBeat: California, Spain and Australia share the listening.
records.dependency: Communication with deep-space missions depends on the Deep Space Network's three complexes.
records.mechanism: Sites spread around the globe keep at least one large dish facing any spacecraft as Earth rotates.
records.bottleneck: Only a handful of very large dishes can hear the faintest signals, and many missions compete for their time.
records.failureConsequence: Losing a complex would leave gaps in coverage, delaying commands and data from distant probes.
records.resilience: Multiple dishes per site, arraying antennas together and partner agencies' stations add capacity.
records.expectedConsequence: missions lose tracking time before they lose contact entirely
visualScenes: Earth rotation handing off between sites
faint signal from a distant probe
editorialTitles: The Three Places That Talk to Deep Space
Why NASA Needs Antennas on Three Continents

facts.claim: The Deep Space Network's facilities are located in California, Madrid in Spain and Canberra in Australia.
Each complex has three or more 34-meter beam waveguide antennas and one 70-meter antenna.
Five of the 34-meter beam waveguide antennas were added in the late 1990s.
The Goldstone complex is about 60 kilometres north of Barstow, California.
The DSN supplied larger antennas for emergency communications such as Apollo 13.

narration.text: Why every deep-space probe depends on 3 sites.
California, Spain and Australia share the listening.
As Earth turns, one site always faces each spacecraft.
Each has a 70-metre dish and several 34-metre dishes.
They even carried emergency links during Apollo 13.
Dozens of missions compete for time on the same few dishes.
So losing one site means losing a third of the sky.

records.coreQuestion: Why do communications satellites sit exactly 35,786 kilometres above the equator?
records.openingLine: These satellites never move in your sky.
records.secondBeat: They orbit exactly as fast as Earth turns.
records.dependency: Satellite TV, weather imaging and many links depend on the single geostationary ring above the equator.
records.mechanism: At 35,786 km altitude, an orbit takes one sidereal day, so the satellite stays over one spot and fixed dishes can point at it.
records.bottleneck: There is only one geostationary ring, and its orbital slots and frequencies are limited and internationally coordinated.
records.failureConsequence: A failed satellite leaves its coverage dark until a spare is moved or a replacement is launched.
records.resilience: In-orbit spares, redundant transponders and end-of-life graveyard orbits protect the ring.
records.expectedConsequence: service in one footprint drops until capacity is moved
editorialTitles: Why Satellites Hover Over One Spot
The 240-Millisecond Delay in Satellite Links

facts.claim: The geostationary altitude is 35,786 kilometres above the equator.
This equates to an orbital speed of 3.07 kilometres per second and an orbital period of 1,436 minutes, one sidereal day.
It takes about 240 ms for a signal to pass from a ground transmitter on the equator to the satellite and back.
Satellites must have a 90% chance of moving over 200 km above the geostationary belt at end of life.
Subtracting Earth's equatorial radius of 6,378 kilometres gives the geostationary altitude.

narration.text: These satellites never move in your sky.
They orbit exactly as fast as Earth turns.
That only works 35,786 kilometres above the equator.
Up there, one orbit takes 1,436 minutes, one sidereal day.
A signal's round trip takes about 240 milliseconds.
At end of life, satellites must climb over 200 kilometres higher.
That's why this one ring above the equator is so crowded and so guarded.

records.topic: Why One Country Supplies Most Rare Earths
records.coreQuestion: How did one country come to supply about 90% of the rare-earth powders the world uses?
records.openingLine: 90% of rare-earth powders came from one country.
records.secondBeat: In 2019, China supplied around 90% of global demand.
records.dependency: Magnets in motors, turbines and electronics depend on separated rare-earth elements.
records.mechanism: Rare earths occur mixed together and must be separated through long chains of chemical extraction steps.
records.bottleneck: Separation capacity is concentrated in one country, and new plants take years to build and qualify.
records.failureConsequence: Export restrictions tighten supply for magnet makers first, then for the products that use them.
records.resilience: New mines and separation plants in other countries, recycling and substitute magnet designs slowly add supply.
records.expectedConsequence: magnet supply tightens first; finished-product shortages lag
editorialTitles: Why Rare Earths Are a Chokepoint
The Chemical Separation Behind Every Magnet

facts.claim: In 2019, China supplied around 90% of the global demand for the 17 rare-earth powders.
Between 1985 and 1995 China increased its share of rare-earth production from 21% to 60%.
As of 2025, the US and Australia produce the second- and third-highest amounts of rare earths, while Brazil has the second-largest reserves.
Promethium, element 61, was produced synthetically in 1945, the last rare-earth element to be discovered.

narration.text: 90% of rare-earth powders came from one country.
In 2019, China supplied around 90% of global demand.
Between 1985 and 1995, its share grew from 21% to 60%.
These 17 elements occur mixed, and separating them is slow chemistry.
They end up in magnets for motors, turbines and electronics.
New separation plants elsewhere take years to build.
That's why an export rule can ripple into car factories.

records.topic: The Metal That Melts in Your Hand and Powers Chips
records.coreQuestion: Why does a metal that melts at 29.76 °C matter so much to semiconductors, and who makes it?
records.openingLine: This metal melts in your hand.
records.secondBeat: Gallium turns liquid at 29.76 degrees Celsius.
records.dependency: Compound semiconductors in LEDs, radio chips and power electronics depend on gallium.
records.mechanism: Gallium is recovered as a by-product of refining other ores, then purified for semiconductor compounds.
records.bottleneck: Primary production is concentrated in one country, and recovery capacity elsewhere is small.
records.failureConsequence: Export restrictions would squeeze chipmakers who rely on gallium compounds before substitutes exist.
records.resilience: Restarting recovery at refineries elsewhere, recycling and stockpiles can add supply over time.
editorialTitles: The Liquid Metal Behind LEDs and Radar Chips
Why Gallium Supply Is a Chokepoint

facts.claim: The melting point of gallium, 29.7646 °C, is used as a temperature reference point.
As of July 2023, China accounted for between 80% and 95% of gallium production.
Germany ceased primary production of gallium in 2016.
Gallium's volume expands by 3.10% when it changes from liquid to solid.
Gallium's boiling point, 2,676 K, is nearly nine times its melting point on the absolute scale.

narration.text: This metal melts in your hand.
Gallium turns liquid at 29.76 degrees Celsius.
Yet it's in LEDs, radio chips and power electronics.
It's mostly recovered as a by-product of refining other ores.
By 2023, China made between 80% and 95% of it.
Germany stopped primary production in 2016.
So one export decision can reach chip factories worldwide.

records.topic: The Battery Metal That Mostly Comes From One Country
records.coreQuestion: Why do so many batteries depend on cobalt mined in the Democratic Republic of the Congo?
records.openingLine: Over 80% of cobalt comes from one country.
records.secondBeat: The Democratic Republic of the Congo mines most of it.
records.dependency: Many lithium-ion battery chemistries depend on refined cobalt.
records.mechanism: Cobalt ore is mined, concentrated and refined into battery-grade chemicals such as cobalt sulfate.
records.bottleneck: Mining is concentrated in one country, so any disruption there moves the whole market.
records.failureConsequence: A supply shock raises battery costs and pushes makers toward cobalt-free chemistries.
records.resilience: Low-cobalt and cobalt-free chemistries, recycling and new mines reduce dependence over time.
records.expectedConsequence: prices react first; chemistry choices shift over years
editorialTitles: Why Batteries Depend on One Country's Cobalt
The Metal Inside Many Rechargeable Batteries

facts.claim: In 2024, cobalt production exceeded 300,000 tons, of which the DRC accounted for more than 80%.
World production in 2016 was 116,000 tonnes, and the DRC alone accounted for more than 50%.
Large deposits were discovered in the Katanga Province in the Congo in 1914.
Cobalt-60 is a commercially important radioisotope used for producing high-energy gamma rays.

narration.text: Over 80% of cobalt comes from one country.
The Democratic Republic of the Congo mines most of it.
World output passed 300,000 tons that year.
Back in 2016, that country's share was just over 50%.
Refined cobalt ends up in many rechargeable batteries.
A disruption there moves prices for battery makers everywhere.
That's why battery chemists keep designing cobalt out.

records.topic: The Gas Behind Chip Lasers That Came From a War Zone
records.coreQuestion: How did most of the world's neon end up coming from Ukraine, and why do chipmakers care?
records.openingLine: 70% of the world's neon came from Ukraine.
records.secondBeat: Then the 2022 invasion hit that supply.
records.dependency: Excimer lasers used in chip lithography depend on high-purity neon gas.
records.mechanism: Neon is a trace gas in air, about 18.2 ppm, captured as a by-product of large air-separation plants.
records.bottleneck: Purification capacity was concentrated in a few plants tied to steel production in Russia and Ukraine.
records.failureConsequence: A cut in neon supply raises costs for laser gas and pushes chipmakers to recycle or source elsewhere.
records.resilience: Neon recycling at fabs, new air-separation capacity and stockpiles reduce exposure.
records.expectedConsequence: gas prices jump first; production continues on stockpiles and recycling
visualScenes: excimer laser in a lithography tool
editorialTitles: Why Chipmakers Worried About Ukraine's Neon
The Trace Gas Inside Chip Lasers

facts.claim: Before the 2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine, about 70% of the global neon supply was produced in Ukraine as a by-product of steel production in Russia.
As of 2020, the company Iceblick, with plants in Odesa and Moscow, supplied 65% of the world's neon.
Neon constitutes about 18.2 ppm of Earth's atmospheric volume.
After 1902, Air Liquide produced industrial quantities of neon as a by-product of air liquefaction.
Neon was discovered in 1898 alongside krypton and xenon.

narration.text: 70% of the world's neon came from Ukraine.
Then the 2022 invasion hit that supply.
Neon is only a tiny trace in the air we breathe.
It's captured as a by-product of giant air-separation plants.
One company once claimed 65% of world supply.
Chip lithography lasers depend on that purified gas.
That's why a war zone can reach a chip factory.

records.topic: The Liquid Helium Keeping MRI Magnets Cold
records.coreQuestion: Why do MRI scanners depend on a liquid that exists only four degrees above absolute zero?
records.openingLine: MRI magnets need helium at −269 degrees.
records.secondBeat: It's liquid helium, only 4.15 kelvin above absolute zero.
records.dependency: Superconducting MRI magnets depend on liquid helium to stay cold enough to superconduct.
records.mechanism: Liquid helium keeps the magnet's coils superconducting, so a strong field runs with no electrical resistance.
records.bottleneck: Helium is a non-renewable by-product of natural gas, and supply comes from a limited number of plants.
records.failureConsequence: Helium shortages raise costs and can delay refills, putting magnets at risk of warming up.
records.resilience: Low-helium sealed magnets, recovery systems and diversified suppliers reduce dependence.
records.expectedConsequence: refill costs rise first; new low-helium designs spread over years
editorialTitles: Why MRI Needs the Coldest Liquid on Earth
The Helium Behind Every MRI Scan

facts.claim: At standard pressure, helium exists as a liquid only at −269 °C (4.15 K).
Liquid helium-4 at its boiling point has a density of about 125 g/L, about one-eighth that of liquid water.
The Large Hadron Collider's superconducting magnets are cooled with 120 tonnes of liquid helium.
Most MRI systems operate at 1.5 T, with commercial systems available between 0.2 and 7 T.

narration.text: MRI magnets need helium at −269 degrees.
It's liquid helium, only 4.15 kelvin above absolute zero.
So that cold keeps the magnet's coils superconducting.
Most scanners run at 1.5 tesla with no electrical resistance.
Physics labs use it too: the Large Hadron Collider holds 120 tonnes.
Helium is a by-product of natural gas, and supply is limited.
That's why hospitals watch helium prices as closely as scans.

records.coreQuestion: How did the world's master kilogram drift, and what replaced it?
records.openingLine: Why the master kilogram lost 50 micrograms.
records.secondBeat: It drifted compared with its own copies over a century.
records.dependency: Every scale, from pharmacies to trade, traces its accuracy back through a chain of calibrations to the definition of the kilogram.
records.mechanism: National labs compared their platinum-iridium copies with the prototype kilogram in Paris during rare verifications.
records.bottleneck: A single physical object defined the unit, so any drift in it silently shifted the whole chain.
records.failureConsequence: A drifting reference means every calibration inherits an error nobody can measure against the reference itself.
records.resilience: Since 2019 the kilogram is defined by a fixed constant of nature, so it can be realised in labs anywhere.
records.expectedConsequence: errors hide inside the reference until an independent definition exposes them
visualScenes: prototype kilogram under glass bell jars
calibration chain from lab to shop scale
editorialTitles: The Kilogram That Mysteriously Lost Mass
Why the Kilogram Was Redefined

facts.claim: The IPK lost perhaps 50 μg of mass over the last century compared with its official copies.
facts.source: Wikipedia — International Prototype of the Kilogram

facts.claim: The only three verifications occurred in 1889, 1948, and 1989.
facts.source: Wikipedia — International Prototype of the Kilogram

facts.claim: The US primary standard K20 had an official mass of 1 kg − 39 μg in 1889.
facts.source: Wikipedia — International Prototype of the Kilogram

facts.claim: The US owns five 90% platinum / 10% iridium kilogram standards.
facts.source: Wikipedia — International Prototype of the Kilogram

facts.claim: Following the 2019 revision of the SI, every base unit except the mole relies on the definition of the second.

narration.text: Why the master kilogram lost 50 micrograms.
It drifted compared with its own copies over a century.
It was checked only three times: 1889, 1948 and 1989.
Nations kept platinum-iridium copies to calibrate against it.
If the master drifts, every scale in the chain drifts with it.
So in 2019, the kilogram was redefined by a constant of nature.
That's why no metal object defines a kilogram anymore.

records.coreQuestion: Why do about 60% of the world's railway lines share one odd track width?
records.openingLine: Why 60% of railways share one odd width.
records.secondBeat: Standard gauge is exactly 1,435 millimetres between the rails.
records.dependency: Through-running trains and cross-border freight depend on shared track gauge.
records.mechanism: Wheelsets are fixed to one rail spacing, so a train can only run where the track matches it.
records.bottleneck: Where gauges differ, cargo must be transferred or wheelsets changed at the border.
records.failureConsequence: A gauge break adds hours, cost and handling to every shipment that crosses it.
records.resilience: Dual-gauge track, variable-gauge wheelsets and transfer terminals soften the break.
editorialTitles: Why Railway Tracks Are 1,435 Millimetres Apart
The Odd Number That Connects Railways

facts.claim: A standard-gauge railway has a track gauge of 1,435 mm (4 ft 8+1⁄2 in).
It is the most widely used track gauge, with about 60% of the lines in the world using it.
Its adoption throughout much of the world allowed interconnectivity and interoperability.
One railway used a different gauge for 15 years before changing to 1,435 mm around 1850.

narration.text: Why 60% of railways share one odd width.
Standard gauge is exactly 1,435 millimetres between the rails.
That's four feet eight and a half inches.
Trains' wheels are fixed to one spacing, so tracks must match.
Sharing it lets trains cross networks without stopping.
Where gauges differ, cargo or wheels must change at the border.
That's why an odd number still decides how freight moves.

records.topic: The Standard Box That Changed World Trade
records.coreQuestion: How did one standard box size let ships, trains and trucks move 20 million containers?
records.openingLine: 20.5 million boxes share the same standard.
records.secondBeat: Intermodal containers fit ships, trains and trucks alike.
records.dependency: Global container shipping depends on standard box sizes and fittings that every crane, ship and truck accepts.
records.mechanism: Standard dimensions and corner fittings let the same box move between ship, rail and road without unpacking.
records.bottleneck: Every crane, cell guide and chassis is built around the standard, so changing it would mean rebuilding the whole system.
records.failureConsequence: A non-standard box cannot use the global network and has to be handled as costly break-bulk cargo.
records.resilience: Because the standard is shared, containers, cranes and ships from any supplier can substitute for each other.
records.expectedConsequence: standardisation makes the system resilient to single suppliers
visualScenes: container moving from ship to train to truck
editorialTitles: The Box That Built Global Trade
Why Every Shipping Container Is the Same Size

facts.claim: In 2012, there were about 20.5 million intermodal containers in the world.
In 1955, trucking magnate Malcom McLean bought Pan-Atlantic Steamship Company to form a container shipping enterprise, later Sea-Land.
A twenty-foot equivalent unit equals one standard 20-foot (6.1 m) long container.
Each container has a unique ISO 6346 reporting mark.
In 1968, McLean began container service to South Vietnam for the US military.

narration.text: 20.5 million boxes share the same standard.
Intermodal containers fit ships, trains and trucks alike.
The unit of trade is the 20-foot box, about 6.1 metres long.
Each carries a unique ISO 6346 code.
Malcom McLean started building the system in 1955.
Now every crane and chassis is built around those sizes.
That's why a box you never see decides what your goods cost.

records.topic: The 12 Digits on Almost Everything You Buy
records.coreQuestion: How does a 12-digit number let every checkout in the world recognise the same product?
records.openingLine: 12 digits identify almost everything you buy.
records.secondBeat: A UPC barcode gives every product its own number.
records.dependency: Retail checkout, inventory and supply-chain tracking depend on globally unique product numbers.
records.mechanism: A central organisation assigns number ranges so each trade item gets a unique code that scanners read in a fraction of a second.
records.bottleneck: The numbering system only works if one organisation coordinates the codes worldwide.
records.failureConsequence: Duplicate or missing codes would break checkout, stock counts and recalls.
records.resilience: A single global registry, check digits and backward-compatible code formats keep the system consistent.
records.expectedConsequence: errors surface at checkout and in inventory first
editorialTitles: The First Thing Ever Scanned at a Checkout
How 12 Digits Run Every Supermarket

facts.claim: A UPC-A consists of 12 digits uniquely assigned to each trade item.
The international GS1 organisation assigns the digits used for both the UPC and the EAN barcode.
The first UPC-marked item scanned at a retail checkout was a 10-pack (50 sticks) of Wrigley's Juicy Fruit gum at the Marsh supermarket in Troy, Ohio.
The first UPC scan took place on 26 June 1974.
UPC data structures are a component of Global Trade Item Numbers and follow the GS1 specification.

narration.text: 12 digits identify almost everything you buy.
A UPC barcode gives every product its own number.
One organisation, GS1, assigns those numbers worldwide.
The first item ever scanned was a pack of Juicy Fruit gum.
That happened in Troy, Ohio, on 26 June 1974.
Duplicate codes would break checkouts, stock counts and recalls.
That's why a registry you never see runs every supermarket.

records.topic: The Day the Internet Outgrew Old Routers
records.coreQuestion: How did one routing-table milestone in 2014 knock parts of the internet offline?
records.openingLine: 15,000 new routes knocked old routers offline.
records.secondBeat: The internet's routing table passed 512,000 entries.
records.dependency: Every packet crossing between networks depends on the Border Gateway Protocol's shared routing table.
records.mechanism: Networks announce which address blocks they can reach, and routers store the full table to choose paths.
records.bottleneck: Older routers had hardware tables sized for about 512,000 routes, a limit the internet was approaching.
records.failureConsequence: When the table crossed the limit, affected routers dropped routes and parts of the internet became unstable for hours.
records.resilience: Router reconfiguration, hardware upgrades and route aggregation raise the ceiling.
editorialTitles: The Day the Internet's Routing Table Broke Old Routers
What Happened on 512k Day

facts.claim: A full IPv4 BGP table as of August 2014 was in excess of 512,000 prefixes, while many older routers had a limit of 512k routing entries.
On impacted routers, the TCAM was by default allocated as 512k IPv4 routes and 256k IPv6 routes.
The announcement of about 15,000 new routes in short order, starting at 07:48 UTC, pushed the table above 512k.
The new routes were reaggregated within 5 minutes, but instability continued for a number of hours.

narration.text: 15,000 new routes knocked old routers offline.
The internet's routing table passed 512,000 entries.
Every network announces which addresses it can reach, using BGP.
Many older routers could only hold 512,000 routes.
It happened in August 2014, starting at 07:48 UTC.
They were fixed within 5 minutes, yet instability lasted hours.
That's why the internet's map can outgrow the machines reading it.

records.topic: The 2.8-Kilometre Channel Asia's Oil Must Pass
records.coreQuestion: Why does so much of Asia's oil squeeze through a channel just 2.8 kilometres wide?
records.openingLine: Why 35% of seaborne oil passes one channel.
records.secondBeat: The Strait of Malacca narrows to just 2.8 kilometres.
records.dependency: Much of East Asia's seaborne oil and gas depends on passage through the Strait of Malacca.
records.mechanism: Ships follow a traffic separation scheme through a long strait that narrows to 2.8 km near Singapore.
records.bottleneck: The largest tankers are too deep for its 25-metre minimum depth, and detours add days.
records.failureConsequence: A blockage would force ships onto longer routes through Indonesian straits, raising costs and delivery times.
records.resilience: Alternative straits, pipelines and strategic reserves cover part of a disruption.
records.expectedConsequence: freight costs rise first as ships reroute
visualScenes: satellite map of the Strait of Malacca
editorialTitles: The Narrow Channel Carrying Asia's Oil
Why the Strait of Malacca Is a Chokepoint

facts.claim: As of 2024, over 35% of oil transported by sea and 20% of gas flowed through the strait.
The strait narrows to only 2.8 km (1.5 nautical miles) wide at the Phillip Channel near southern Singapore.
The draught of some of the largest ships exceeds the strait's minimum depth of 25 metres.
Roughly 80% of China's imported crude oil passes through the strait.
There have been 34 shipwrecks in the local traffic separation scheme channel.

narration.text: Why 35% of seaborne oil passes one channel.
The Strait of Malacca narrows to just 2.8 kilometres.
That's the Phillip Channel, near southern Singapore.
About 80% of China's crude imports come this way.
Its minimum depth is 25 metres, too shallow for the biggest tankers.
Any detour through other straits adds time and cost.
That's why a channel this narrow shapes an entire region's energy.
